scripts.script:
Before Phyrexia had a name, a single wound opened the way to it.

Nine years before the Thran-Phyrexian War, Halcyon drew its power from a mana rig buried beneath a dormant volcano. Glacian, the empire?s greatest artificer, had built the machinery. Its crystal orbs were broken into powerstones, jewels charged by sunlight and volcanic heat. Some would raise the foundations of Rebbec?s temple above the city.

The process was dangerous, but Glacian trusted machines more than people. When the great orb finished charging, he broke it and stood among a thousand new stones. Then an Untouchable?one of the exiles confined to the Caves of the Damned?seized a stone and drove it into Glacian?s belly. The riot had reached the heart of Halcyon?s prosperity.

At the infirmary, the healers? magic failed. The stone grew hotter inside the wound. Rebbec reached into her husband?s body and pulled it free herself. Glacian survived long enough to speak of the stones meant for her temple. Rebbec could think only of keeping him alive.

Then the infirmary shook. Another powerstone failed, and half the building was destroyed.

The empire?s greatest invention had wounded its maker and shattered the place built to heal him. The attacker was still unnamed. The cause of Glacian?s illness was unknown. Halcyon had power enough to lift a city into the sky, but no answer for the sickness spreading beneath it.

That answer would bring an exile home. His name was Yawgmoth.
scripts.notes: Compact two-minute regeneration from The Thran, chapters 1?3. The attacker remains unnamed until the chapter 3 identification of Gix.

scripts.script:
The Thran Empire did not welcome Yawgmoth with trumpets. It summoned him because its greatest artificer was dying.

After years of exile, the physician condemned by Halcyon was called back to the capital. He was given no skyship and no escort. He walked the long highway while cargo vessels crossed the sky above him.

By the time he reached the volcanic road below Halcyon, the insult had become another fact to be measured. The empire needed him. It had simply not yet learned what that need would cost.

Yawgmoth had been exiled with the eugenicists after a century of civil conflict. The artificers trusted machines. The eugenicists studied the machine of the body. When Halcyon's imperial party prevailed, the losing physicians were made into scapegoats.

Yawgmoth and two hundred followers wandered among peoples the Thran considered primitive, studying disease in lizardfolk, minotaurs, goblins, orcs, lepers, and lunatics. Exile gave him time to refine one conviction: disease was a physical invasion, and the body could be studied and cured.

Now Glacian was rotting from within, and the empire had finally come to ask whether the exile had been right.

At Halcyon's gate stood figures of the ideal Thran man and woman, carved in the empire's image of perfect health. Beneath them, an artificial stream ran across the threshold to wash dust from every visitor's feet.

Yawgmoth knew the statues were a lie. He had opened bodies. Healthy flesh was never so perfect.

Then Rebbec came to meet him. She wore council robes that sat awkwardly on a woman accustomed to work. She had fought to revoke his banishment and had come directly from the infirmary.

Between them ran the little stream. Rebbec knelt and washed the road from Yawgmoth's feet herself. For a man discarded by the empire, it was a small ceremony. It was also the first sign that Halcyon might let him cross its threshold.

Rebbec took Yawgmoth through Halcyon's ascending terraces to the apartment prepared near the infirmary. There he began the work the empire had summoned him to perform.

Glacian's illness was called phthisis, a progressive degeneration that resisted every healer and worsened under magic. Removing the powerstone from his chair had cleared some lesions, but the disease remained. Yawgmoth found many small organisms in Glacian's samples, yet none seemed to be the primary cause.

He suspected the answer lay where the wound had begun. Glacian's attacker came from the Caves of the Damned, the sealed underworld beneath Halcyon's mana rig. If the attacker carried the disease, the caves might hold the truth.

The entrance to the caves was guarded by men who believed the darkness below belonged to monsters. Yawgmoth brought rope, lanterns, scalpels, flasks, and poisoned weapons. The captain warned him that the Untouchables would kill him.

Yawgmoth tied his rope, stepped into the shaft, and descended. His lantern made only a small circle of light. Bones lay below the switchback path. A frightened woman hid beneath a stalagmite as he passed. He did not slow.

He entered the caves as a physician who believed the people below might contain the evidence he needed.

At the bottom, the darkness had a population. Pale faces gathered beneath the overhangs. Their clothes were filthy, their bodies thin, their eyes widened by lives spent without sunlight. At their center stood a giant who demanded to know why a healer had come armed with swords.

Yawgmoth told them he was searching for a man with a deadly disease, one that had spread through their people.

The caves were not empty refuse beneath a glorious city. They were a society abandoned to confinement. Halcyon had sealed the exits and continued sending prisoners downward. Now Yawgmoth saw both a danger and an answer.

Yawgmoth found Gix among the infected. The Untouchable had stabbed Glacian during the riot at the mana rig. By the time Yawgmoth reached him, Gix was a living skeleton, ravaged by the same disease that consumed his victim.

The wound, the powerstone, the lesions, the caves, and the city above them began to form a single chain. Yawgmoth brought Gix back to Halcyon. There, attacker and victim were placed under the same care.

The empire had summoned a doctor. It had given him two famous bodies, a frightened city, and access to the people beneath it.

The next morning, Yawgmoth worked on both patients. He cut away diseased tissue, applied salves, inserted strips of metal, and recorded what the body accepted or rejected. He did not treat pain as a moral boundary. He treated it as interference.

Gix called him a poisoner. Glacian understood the more dangerous truth: Yawgmoth was trying to understand the disease, and every wound was another question asked of the flesh.

The council had expelled him as a threat. Now it watched his work and offered aid because the disease had reached Halcyon's greatest artificer. The doors opened. The instruments arrived. The observers gathered. Power had begun to follow the man who returned without an escort.

That day, Yawgmoth was expected at the launch of the Thran Temple's floating foundation. He left the infirmary in clothes Rebbec had provided and rose through Halcyon's terraces in a powerstone sedan chair. The city had built upward because there was no room left to build outward. Its temple promised to go higher still: a plane of tens of thousands of powerstones above Council Boulevard. When Rebbec stood on the Council Hall dome, her image was thrown through the stones and projected across the city. Halcyon saw its architect become a figure of light.

Yawgmoth had studied bodies among the exiled and forgotten. Now he saw a civilization project an image of its own perfection.

When the foundation rose, gray stone became color. Rebbec leaped from the dome and landed upon the floating temple, and Halcyon answered with a roar.

Yawgmoth did not wait for permission. He crossed the rooftops, climbed to the pinnacle of Council Hall, and leaped across the empty space. He landed in Rebbec's arms. For a breath, the exile and the architect stood together above the city that had rejected him. Glacian watched from below, too ill to bear the powerstone glare. The Thran had called Yawgmoth back to save a dying man. Now he stood at the center of their dream.

Powerstones could heal. They could also burn.

scripts.script:
Glacian woke from his coma diminished in body but not in ambition. Machines breathed for him. Goblins maintained the apparatus around his chair. His memory came and went, yet he continued to design weapons and powerstone defenses. He believed Yawgmoth was using his work to prepare a private army, and he declared that he would fight both the physician and the death consuming him.

Below the city, Gix had reached the same conclusion by another path. The serum was being diluted. More patients arrived in the quarantine caves, while fewer healthy people were allowed to ascend. Gix urged rebellion. The refugees wanted escape more than revolution, and Yawgmoth used that division against them. He watched the route Gix used to lead people out, ambushed the refugees, and kept Gix alive because a predictable enemy was more useful than a dead one.

When the next uprising came, Yawgmoth had already prepared the city. A crystal angel fell upon the attackers at the infirmary. Guards and healers closed the streets. The elders, frightened by the scale of the violence, gave Yawgmoth command of the Halcyte guard. He armed the soldiers with powerstone armor, poisoned swords, and a network that allowed him to monitor the city.

Gix stole the armor of a fallen guard and turned Yawgmoth?s technology against its maker. The revolt still failed. Its survivors had not defeated Yawgmoth; they had given him the authority to direct the whole city.

Two years before the Ibr?n-Phyrexian War, Halcyon held a feast to celebrate recovery, the temple?s completion, and the supposed end of the incursions. The celebration was interrupted by Prince Delsuum and a coalition of dwarves, elves, viashino, minotaurs, cat people, and humans. They accused Yawgmoth of using plague and rebellion to rise from exile to power. They demanded his extradition.

The council rejected the demand. Rebbec voted against it. Yawgmoth answered the foreign accusation with a domestic seizure. He declared that the empire was under attack, dissolved the council, and assumed command.

His rise had not been one decision. It had accumulated through wounds, treatments, shortages, fear, and the promise of protection. Each crisis had made the next concentration of power appear necessary. By the time the Thran understood the shape of his rule, the old government had already become an obstacle he could remove in public.

scripts.script:
Yawgmoth?s seizure of the empire left the rebel elders imprisoned and the city-states preparing for war. Rebbec and Glacian summoned Dyfed, the woman who had entered Halcyon as a stranger and revealed herself as a planeswalker. They asked her to carry the elders and Glacian?s goblins to safety. Dyfed took them to another world, later identified as Mercadia, and left them to survive outside the empire they had once governed.

Glacian was not carried with them. His body had deteriorated beyond what his machines could sustain, and Yawgmoth moved him into the quarantine system. The caves were clean, numbered, and closely watched. Their order promised healing, but the patients were also subjects in an expanding program.

Above them, Rebbec watched Yawgmoth place weapons on Halcyon?s gates. He spoke of necessity. She saw the city she had designed becoming a fortress. When Dyfed returned, Yawgmoth asked whether she had found the world he wanted.

She took Yawgmoth and Rebbec beyond Dominaria. The passage through the Blind Eternities was violent even under a planeswalker?s protection. They emerged in an artificial world shaped like a series of vast spheres. Its former master, a dragon, was dead. The world remained, waiting for another will to inhabit it.

Yawgmoth saw a refuge, a laboratory, and a weapon. Dyfed explained that the spheres could be linked to Halcyon and that a permanent passage might be built. Yawgmoth named the world Phyrexia. The name was not yet attached to an empire of transformed bodies, but the intention was already larger than a hospital or a shelter.

The war preparations accelerated. Halcyon armed its gates with ray cannons, its walls with ballistae and mirrors, and its airships with powerstone weapons. Yawgmoth?s forces prepared the Null Sphere. In the midst of this work, he opened Glacian?s wound and removed a sliver of powerstone encapsulated in the artificer?s flesh. Glacian?s phthisis eased, but the discovery strengthened Yawgmoth?s control over both the patient and the technology built from his designs.

Within Phyrexia, Yawgmoth?s consciousness spread through the world. Patients became newts. Buildings grew into forms that belonged to the plane. Medical work became transformation, and transformation became a vision of a new race.

Rebbec had once believed that artifice might lift the Thran beyond disease and war. She now watched the same ambition take root beneath the world. The refuge had become a kingdom in preparation, and its ruler no longer imagined a limit to what it could become.

scripts.script:
The war reached its decisive stage at the Megheddon Defile. Rebbec stayed in the quarantine caves with Glacian, whose body had improved after Yawgmoth removed the powerstone sliver, while his mind continued to fracture. Above them, Yawgmoth positioned the Null Sphere and waited for the Thran Alliance to enter the narrow ground.

The device drew power from the battlefield. A killing cloud spread over the army, stripping away soldiers, machines, stone, and earth. When the cloud was drawn into the Null Sphere, Yawgmoth redirected the energy toward Phyrexia and the empire?s artifact engines. The battle was no longer a contest between armies. It had become a means of feeding the world he had built.

More fleets arrived from the west. Halcyon?s defenders fought from the walls and the air. Yawgmoth?s forces had the weapons of Glacian?s designs and the obedience of a state organized around fear. Gix, once the leader of the Untouchables, now served as a commander within the Phyrexian hierarchy. His rebellion had ended in the position that gave him the greatest power over the people he once sought to free.

Phyrexia?s transformation program became visible during the siege. People who had entered the world seeking treatment emerged altered: bodies reinforced, reshaped, and made obedient to the machinery around them. Rebbec saw that the language of improvement concealed a destruction of the people being improved. Yawgmoth did not see monsters. He saw the beginning of gods.

When the Thran armies refused his terms, Yawgmoth turned to the stone-chargers. Their bombs fell from the sky and erased armies across the desert. The killing clouds rose around Halcyon. The Null Sphere was forced upward by an old artificer who sacrificed himself and the command crew to keep the device from drawing the entire cloud into the city.

The temple could not save the people who had gathered there. Carried by the force of the clouds, it rose above Halcyon and broke apart, scattering crystal and refugees over the doomed city. The image of the temple as a promise of ascent ended in destruction.

The Thran civilization did not fall in one blow. It was dismantled by a sequence of weapons, decisions, and compromises. Yawgmoth made each catastrophe serve the next stage of his plan. When the clouds closed over Halcyon, the question was no longer whether the city would survive. It was who would be forced to survive inside the world he had prepared.

scripts.script:
The killing clouds descended through Halcyon. Stone became powder. Wood vanished. People ran toward any opening that led downward, and enemies who would once have killed one another fled side by side through the dark. The old city above had become impossible to inhabit.

Rebbec guided refugees toward the caves. They included Thran citizens, goblins, dwarves, elves, minotaurs, cat people, and the sick who had been abandoned in the old quarantine system. Their differences mattered less than the white cloud behind them. Below the city, the only apparent road to safety led through a portal into Phyrexia.

Yawgmoth stood beyond the gateway with altered soldiers around him. He opened his hands and welcomed the refugees as his children. The promise of shelter concealed the transformation waiting on the other side. Rebbec understood that the refuge was also a border crossing into Yawgmoth?s new order.

Glacian remained behind in the mana rig. His body had been sustained by machines, but the war had stripped away the future he had been building. When Rebbec found him, he was dead. Beneath the wound Yawgmoth had made, however, she discovered two charged stones glowing inside him. They were not an explanation that could restore his life. They were the last connection between the artificer, the portal, and the world Yawgmoth had claimed.

Yawgmoth returned to the cave and promised that he could heal them. Rebbec no longer believed the promise. She understood what healing meant in Phyrexia, and what it had already cost the people who accepted it. He reached for her, but the choice before her was not between two equal refuges. It was between surrendering the gateway and leaving Yawgmoth?s world beyond it.

Rebbec carried Glacian?s stones to the mirror pedestal. The portal answered with light. The crystals in the cave blazed. Machines stirred around the gateway, and for a moment Halcyon could still see Phyrexia through the opening.

Then Rebbec placed the stones in their sconces. The passage failed. The sky, the world, Yawgmoth, and Glacian vanished behind a wall of stone. His final cry echoed through the caves, but the gateway did not reopen.

Rebbec left the darkness alone. She had not saved the empire. She had not healed her husband. She had closed the road by which Yawgmoth could return, and the cost of that act was the knowledge that the world beyond the seal still existed.

The Thran story ended with a door shut between two ruins. On one side lay the remains of Halcyon. On the other, Phyrexia waited with its ruler, its refugees, and all the consequences of the choices that had brought it into being.
